section_summary: This section combines wartime intelligence on the location and condition of Japanese industrial facilities with extensive planning for the treatment of heavy industry after surrender. Its central policy paper weighs demilitarization, minimum civilian needs, economic recovery, and reparations, while later correspondence and press clippings consider Japan’s dependence on foreign trade and prospective return to consumer-goods exports. The section concludes with SCAP’s first postwar industrial inventory, detailing the surviving capacity of Japan’s textile industries.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Mitsubishi influence in the Nitchitsu combine
subfiles.from: Robert P. Terrill, Commodities Division, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests clarification of the alleged extent of Mitsubishi influence over the Nitchitsu chemical combine.
subfiles.summary: Terrill cites Grajdanzev’s 1943 memorandum, which described the expansion of Mitsubishi and Noguchi interests in Chosen Chisso Hiryo. Departmental research found little evidence of substantial Mitsubishi ownership or management influence in its parent, Nippon Chisso Hiryo, and suggested that Sumitomo connections might be more significant. Terrill asks whether Noguchi’s earlier Mitsubishi relationship had been revived during the war.

subfiles.title: Location of Japanese Industries
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits intelligence obtained in Santiago concerning the location of Japanese industries.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards a memorandum based on information from persons who had left Japan since 1940. He states that the information was also supplied to the Foreign Economic Administration, the American Embassy in Santiago, naval intelligence, and Army G-2.

subfiles.title: Japanese Industry
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation reporting in Santiago
subfiles.to: Department of State and other United States agencies
subfiles.about: Reports interviews with diplomats, journalists, and former residents concerning Japanese industrial dispersion and specific facilities.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Chilean and Peruvian diplomats and writers who had recently returned from Japan and records Armando Labra’s observations on household-based subcontracting and severe food shortages. Eugenio and Miguel Sisikin provide locations for aircraft-related construction, the Datsun automobile factory, the Asano shipyard, subterranean aircraft hangars, and a synthetic-oil plant. The information was dated and fragmentary because the sources had left Japan between 1940 and 1943.

subfiles.title: Telegram on coordination of Japanese munitions industry
subfiles.from: Harrison, Bern
subfiles.about: Reports German press coverage of a Japanese decision to consolidate and control munitions production.
subfiles.summary: A Tokyo despatch reported that the Japanese Cabinet had decided to coordinate the munitions industry more closely with the worsening war situation. Factories were to be consolidated by type and location, and the government could assume management of privately owned munitions plants when necessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese war-industry reorganization
subfiles.from: Harrison, Bern
subfiles.about: Summarizes German press reports on measures to expand Japanese war production.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports measures intended to increase production as the war approached Japan. These included redirecting coal and raw-material supplies, classifying machine tools as an essential armaments industry, raising prices and mineral premiums, granting mines preferential labor treatment, and transferring some factory workers to mining.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the dollar-yen rate
subfiles.from: D. M. Phelps
subfiles.about: Notes Treasury approval of a proposed dollar-yen exchange rate communicated to General Crist.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that the dollar-yen rate had been discussed repeatedly. It records that Treasury approved the proposal contained in a letter to General Crist.

subfiles.title: Industry in Japan
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits an intelligence report based on interviews with Chilean journalists and a diplomatic official formerly stationed in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hoover highlights the enclosure’s information about a major shipyard at Hakata and Japanese coal mines and hydroelectric facilities in Asia. Particular attention is directed to the Kirin plant, reportedly intended to supply electricity throughout Manchuria. The report was also shared with the American Embassy in Santiago, the Foreign Economic Administration, naval intelligence, and the War Department.

subfiles.title: Japanese Industry
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation reporting in Santiago
subfiles.to: Department of State and other United States agencies
subfiles.about: Compiles source reports on major Japanese and continental Asian industrial centers, transport, mines, power facilities, and copper refineries.
subfiles.summary: Sources described the Osaka–Nagoya–Kobe and Tokyo–Yokohama regions as Japan’s principal manufacturing centers and identified shipyards, naval facilities, the Shimonoseki–Moji tunnel, Manchurian mines, aircraft factories, and the large Kirin hydroelectric plant. Another source listed Japanese-built copper refineries in Japan and Korea and discussed Japan’s dependence on imported Chilean copper. The memorandum also comments on Japan’s electrified railways, poor intercity roads, Hokkaido fishing ports, and coastal shipbuilding.

subfiles.title: Request for a paper on heavy industry in the Japanese economy
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests a short draft statement on the role of heavy industry in Japan for the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee.
subfiles.summary: Martin confirms earlier conversations with Johnstone and Daugherty about a planned series of policy papers. He asks for a draft of no more than ten pages covering the agreed definition of heavy industry in the Japanese economy.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for “Heavy Industry in Japan”
subfiles.from: Mr. Lockhart
subfiles.about: Routes the paper titled “Heavy Industry in Japan,” with Mr. Deimel also identified.
subfiles.summary: This brief internal form records the circulation of the heavy-industry policy paper. It contains no substantive discussion beyond the paper’s title and routing information.

subfiles.title: Heavy Industry in Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Develops proposed United States occupation policy toward Japanese heavy industry, balancing demilitarization, civilian needs, recovery, and reparations.
subfiles.summary: The paper recommends industry-by-industry estimates of demilitarization requirements, minimum civilian needs, economic-recovery requirements, and possible reparations claims. Essential security controls would receive priority, but Japan should retain enough industrial capacity to sustain subsistence, reconstruction, foreign trade, and a viable peaceful economy; 1931 and 1936 production levels are proposed as reference points. It analyzes heavy industry’s growth, employment, dependence on imported raw materials, government subsidies, and integration with transport and electric power, while warning that wholesale elimination would cause mass unemployment and economic distress. The paper proposes selective restriction of key industries, removal of subsidies, supervised use or conversion of facilities, and reparations only after demilitarization and minimum Japanese needs had been met.

subfiles.title: Application for an industrial-control position in defeated Japan
subfiles.from: A. F. Barnard
subfiles.to: Foreign Service Bureau, Department of State
subfiles.about: Applies for an administrative position overseeing aircraft, steel, or manufacturing industries in Japan or another defeated Axis country.
subfiles.summary: Barnard states that Congressman Harry L. Towe recommended that he contact the Department. He emphasizes his production, engineering, and factory-administration experience and encloses a résumé in support of his application.

subfiles.title: Résumé of Experience — A. F. Barnard
subfiles.from: A. F. Barnard
subfiles.to: Foreign Service Bureau, Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Barnard’s education, metallurgical employment, aircraft-materials work, and professional committee service.
subfiles.summary: Barnard lists a metallurgical-engineering degree from Lehigh University and experience with Crucible Steel, Columbia Steel, and Vultee Aircraft. His work encompassed steel production, quality control, alloy sales, aircraft materials, welding, laboratory management, process engineering, and manufacturing troubleshooting. He also participated in professional bodies concerned with metals, welding, armor plate, and aeronautical materials.

subfiles.title: Reply to A. F. Barnard regarding employment in Japan
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Directs Barnard’s employment inquiry to the War Department’s Civil Affairs Division.
subfiles.summary: Dickover acknowledges Barnard’s application for work connected with industrial controls in Japan. Because early Allied authority would be exercised through military agencies, he recommends applying to the Civil Affairs Division of the War Department.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 25549: Japan’s Industrial Future
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Transmits and summarizes two Manchester Guardian articles on Japan’s long-term industrial future and Western trade.
subfiles.summary: Allison explains that the articles review Japan’s prewar dependence on manufactured exports to pay for food and raw materials and assess the consequences of losing its overseas territories and much of its heavy industry. The Guardian argues that Japan may have to concentrate on textiles and other consumer goods, creating renewed competition for Western industry. It nevertheless considers Japanese exports necessary to prevent famine and despair in Japan and to supply affordable goods to impoverished Asian consumers.

subfiles.title: Manchester Guardian clipping: “Japan’s Industrial Future—I: Her Reliance on Foreign Trade”
subfiles.from: Manchester Guardian correspondent
subfiles.about: Reviews the prewar structure of Japan’s economy and its dependence on imported food, raw materials, and export markets.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that postwar Japan’s large population would be confined to resource-poor home islands after the loss of Korea, Formosa, and privileges in Manchuria and China. It describes the limits of Japanese agriculture, the importance of colonial food imports, and the expansion of textiles, metals, engineering, and consumer-goods industries. Because most industrial raw materials came from abroad, Japan’s employment and living standards depended on increasing exports of manufactured goods and shipping services.

subfiles.title: Manchester Guardian clipping: “Japan’s Industrial Future—II: Must She Export More Textiles?”
subfiles.from: Manchester Guardian correspondent
subfiles.about: Considers whether postwar Japan must rebuild a large consumer-goods export trade, particularly in textiles.
subfiles.summary: The article predicts that the loss of colonies, heavy industry, merchant shipping, and raw-silk markets would force Japan to rely much more heavily on exported textiles and miscellaneous consumer goods. Such a strategy could renew severe competition with Lancashire and other Western industries. The writer nevertheless argues that blocking Japanese exports could produce famine and instability in the Far East while denying poorer Asian populations access to inexpensive goods.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 118: Transmission of Summaries of Industrial Inventories
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the first seven SCAP summaries of twenty-three inventories of Japanese industry.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson encloses the first seven industrial-inventory summaries prepared by SCAP’s Industrial and Research Divisions for Ambassador Edwin W. Pauley. He notes that the summaries had already been released publicly and were probably available in Washington, but sends them for the Department’s convenience.

subfiles.title: Summaries of Industrial Inventories
subfiles.from: Public Relations Office, General Headquarters, United States Army Forces, Pacific
subfiles.about: Announces publication of the first seven SCAP inventories of Japanese industry.
subfiles.summary: The release states that the Industrial and Research Divisions of SCAP’s Economic and Scientific Section completed twenty-three industrial inventories on December 1 for Ambassador Edwin W. Pauley. It presents the first seven summaries and promises release of the remaining sixteen when completed.

subfiles.title: Industrial Inventory No. 1: The Textile Industry
subfiles.from: Industrial and Research Divisions, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.to: Edwin W. Pauley and the public
subfiles.about: Quantifies surviving Japanese capacity and projected output in silk, cotton, rayon, wool, flax, and China-grass textiles.
subfiles.summary: The inventory reports Japanese plans to devote silk facilities chiefly to exportable raw silk and gives estimates for mulberry acreage, cocoons, reeling basins, looms, and dyeing and finishing capacity. Historical tables show the wartime contraction of sericulture, silk mills, raw-silk exports, and staple-fibre production. It also records operational spindles, looms, and annual output capacities for cotton, staple fibre, rayon, artificial silk, worsted, wool, flax, and China grass. Major Harold S. Tate and Lieutenant Frank J. Collins directed preparation of the textile and raw-silk sections.
